video.title: Fantasy Basketball Statistical Correlations & Why Turnovers Suck

summary: Josh Lloyd ran Pearson correlations between the 9 categories, using last season's top 200 players in per-game value. In points leagues, fantasy points line up most closely with usage (0.826) and then minutes, so usage matters more there than in category leagues. In category leagues, points and assists are the most strongly linked pair, then threes and FT%. Together these explain why the guard build (points, threes, assists, FT%) works. The big man build (rebounds, blocks, FG%) only links three categories, so it is harder to pull off. Steals, blocks and rebounds are the most independent categories. Turnovers are the most tied to other categories and help almost nothing, since the turnovers track points and assists so closely. His conclusion: in head-to-head leagues that are not games-capped, ignore turnovers except as a tiebreaker between near-identical players. Roto and games-capped leagues are exceptions.

rules.text: In points leagues, minutes and usage are the simplest way to predict fantasy points. Choosing between two players on those two factors gets you about 80% of the way to the right answer.
rules.quote: minutes and which player will have more usage, and you're 80% of the way there

rules.text: Usage matters more in points leagues than in category leagues, though it helps in both.
rules.quote: usage becomes more important in points leagues than it is in category leagues

rules.text: Points and assists come together. If you target high-points players, you usually get assists too, and the reverse is also true.
rules.quote: if you go for higher points players, you will usually bring assists along with it

rules.text: The guard build (points, threes, assists, steals, FT%) is common because its categories reinforce each other.
rules.quote: Points, threes, assists, steals, and free throws is the general guard build.

rules.text: The big man build is harder to execute because only rebounds, blocks and FG% move together.
rules.quote: part of the reason why the the big man build is harder to execute is that that's only three categories

rules.text: Steals are the swing category. They do not tie strongly into either the guard build or the big man build.
rules.quote: we always talk about steals as being the swing number

rules.text: A big man build does not naturally bring steals or low turnovers with it. Blocks and turnovers are not correlated.
rules.quote: Steals aren't getting brought along. And low turnovers aren't necessarily getting brought along either.

rules.text: Threes and FG% pull against each other, so adding threes to a big man build is hard.
rules.quote: more threes means lower field goal percentage. Higher field goal percentage means lower threes.

rules.text: Winning head-to-head categories takes margin. Being barely above average in categories that are negatively correlated leaves you exposed to schedule and injury swings.
rules.quote: part of having success in head-to-head categories is having margin, then you're cooked

rules.text: A small positive z-score in a category (like 0.7) wins only about 55% of the time. A large one (like 2.5) wins about 85%. Build big buffers.
rules.quote: If you get a Z score of 2.5 in your assists, you're going to win 85% of the time

rules.text: Being strong in both FG% and FT% is very hard. Barely winning both is fragile, and putting resources into it leaves you short elsewhere.
rules.quote: one less game from your free throw volume at anchor means that now you've lost the category

rules.text: Players who combine categories that are not normally correlated (like rebounds and assists) carry extra value.
rules.quote: So, players who do the low correlation things are pretty useful.

rules.text: A low-volume build of threes, steals, blocks, FG% and FT% is very hard to pull off, because those categories do not drag each other along.
rules.quote: So, going for like a low volume build a threes steals, blocks, field goals, free throws really tough to pull off

rules.text: Steals are one of the most abundant categories on the waiver wire, and they create oddities in standard 9-cat rankings.
rules.quote: steals are one of the most abundant categories off the waiver wire

rules.text: Maximizing FG% or working hard to keep turnovers low hurts the rest of a fantasy team.
rules.quote: turnovers low, is pretty detrimental to your overall fantasy team. That's what that means.

rules.text: In head-to-head leagues, the speaker ignores turnovers completely.
rules.quote: Cuz you know when I am talking head-to-head leagues, I am telling you I do not care about turnovers.

rules.text: Exception: turnovers matter to a degree in roto leagues.
rules.quote: You are playing in a roto league, turnovers are one of the categories. It is important.

rules.text: Games-capped leagues are a little different, but the correlations still apply.
rules.quote: if I'm playing a games cup league, a little bit different. It's a little bit different.

rules.text: Turnovers are the only negative counting stat in default fantasy formats. Streaming to max games played naturally raises turnovers, so chasing low turnovers fights the head-to-head game.
rules.quote: That's why we stream. Streaming is anti-turnovers. We want more games played than our opponent

rules.text: Injuries and schedule disadvantages automatically lower your turnovers, so you often win turnovers anyway in weeks when you are short on games.
rules.quote: If one of your guys gets injured, he accumulates zero turnovers.

rules.text: Using turnovers as a tiebreaker between two otherwise identical players is fine.
rules.quote: I got no problem if you want to use turnovers between two identical players

rules.text: The speaker's Durant ranking system for head-to-head leagues leaves out turnovers.
rules.quote: I'm not including turnovers in it cuz if you want to win a head-to-head league
